about.title: About Me
about.intro: Technology shapes how people think, work, and interact with the world. I care about building systems that do that thoughtfully.
about.body1: I studied Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Toronto, with a minor in Business and Artificial Intelligence. Since then, my work has moved through product, platform, and infrastructure — from financial technology and operational systems at Coinbase, to developer tooling at Thomson Reuters, to customer-facing systems at Amazon.
about.body2: What interests me is not software in the abstract. It is software as part of something larger: the systems people use to work, decide, trust, and move through complexity. Software is never just software. It lives inside the world, and at its best, it makes that world clearer, more reliable, and easier to act within. To me, good engineering is not only about performance or scale, but about judgment, elegance, and the ability to create technology people can genuinely trust.
about.body3: That is the standard I care about. I want to build systems that matter — systems whose value is felt beyond the codebase. I am not interested in technology as decoration. I want my work to hold its weight in the world outside it.

coinbase.title: Software Engineer
coinbase.summary1: As a Software Engineer at Coinbase, I worked on blockchain infrastructure, internal engineering tools, and AI-assisted systems for operations in a large-scale financial technology environment. Much of my work sat close to the production layer of the business, where software needed to be reliable, observable, and capable of supporting customers’ needs around the clock.
coinbase.summary2: A significant part of my role involved supporting node operations across more than 60 blockchain protocols—this included handling client upgrades and security patches, improving deployment workflows, and coordinating network-level changes. Through this work, I gained much deeper experience with Docker, Helm, Kubernetes, and Datadog, while learning the practical discipline required to operate distributed services where downtime, misconfiguration, or delayed response can carry meaningful consequences.
coinbase.summary3: Coinbase was also the first place where AI became a meaningful part of my daily work as an engineer. I used it to help with debugging, planning implementations, exploring unfamiliar systems, and moving through development tasks more quickly. At the same time, I became very aware of its limitations. AI was most valuable when guided by someone who understood the architecture, constraints, failure modes, nuances, and operational context of the domain. That insight made me a more effective engineer and reinforced my belief that no machine can replace the judgment of someone who has lived with the consequences of the systems they build.
coinbase.summary4: Building on those lessons, I led one of my main projects: an LLM-powered operational knowledge system that unified protocol, incident, and infrastructure data from multiple sources into a single interface for engineers. To achieve this, I worked on MCP integrations, REST APIs, scheduled ingestion workflows, a React frontend, and LangGraph orchestration. The aim was simple: make it easier for engineers to find the information they needed without searching across a collection of disconnected tools.
coinbase.summary5: During my time there, I also built an internal incident response tool that used Datadog integrations to connect infrastructure metrics, service health, and alerts into a clearer investigation workflow. These two projects arose from the same problem I observed repeatedly: during incidents, engineers often had plenty of data points at their disposal but insufficient meaningful context. The real value was not in showing more information, but in helping people understand what mattered and act faster with greater confidence.
coinbase.summary6: All in all, I leave Coinbase with a stronger foundation in production infrastructure, a more disciplined approach to building and operating reliable systems, and a clearer understanding of how to use AI to become a more capable engineer—not a less necessary one.

amazon.title: Software Development Engineer Intern
amazon.summary: As a Software Development Engineer Intern at Amazon, I led the creation of a mobile web feature using React and Redux to help advertisers visualize campaign performance, boosting user engagement and conversion rates by 10%. In addition to development, I conducted design reviews, facilitated User Acceptance Testing (UAT), and executed UI tests to ensure an optimal user experience and the successful release of a bug-free feature. After its launch, I evaluated the feature's impact on user engagement and load times using Weblab, which revealed widespread adoption and minimal latency across different global regions. This experience allowed me to engage deeply with the entire software development lifecycle, from initial concept and design to post-launch maintenance and performance analysis. It equipped me with the skills necessary to effectively create and develop new software solutions. The positive outcomes for customers and the feature's permanent integration into Amazon's website stand as a testament to the value and impact of this work.

thomsonReuters.title: Software Developer Intern
thomsonReuters.summary1: As a Software Developer Intern at Thomson Reuters, I worked on web applications using AWS, C#, .NET, and Angular. A large part of my role involved designing and improving REST APIs, with a strong focus on reliability, scalability, and established industry practices. This work improved the usability and performance of several services while creating a stronger foundation for future backend development.
thomsonReuters.summary2: As I became more comfortable in this area, I took on the challenge of automating onboarding processes, improving internal workflows, implementing secure token exchange systems, and managing user sessions. This gave me a much deeper understanding of modern authorization protocols such as OAuth and of the principles behind identity and access management (IAM). My responsibilities also extended beyond the backend. I helped design and develop responsive, user-friendly interfaces that created a smoother experience for users. Working across both sides of the application gave me a more complete understanding of how technical decisions move through an entire system—an understanding I have continued to build on ever since.
thomsonReuters.summary3: Beyond the technical work, I took an active leadership role within the team’s Agile process, regularly facilitating daily stand-ups, sprint planning sessions, and retrospectives. These experiences strengthened my ability to communicate clearly, organize work, and help a team move toward a shared goal. Looking back, the internship did more than improve my software engineering skills. It taught me how to contribute with confidence, collaborate across cultures and time zones, and grow within a dynamic international team.

splitz.hero: A minimal Google Chrome extension that helps users manage tabs efficiently and reduce browsing clutter.
splitz.description1: In my quest for a more organized browsing experience, I found myself frustrated with the clutter of disorganized, open tabs in Google Chrome. Unable to find a suitable solution, I decided to take matters into my own hands and created Splitz, a Chrome extension designed to help users manage tabs efficiently and have a better experience browsing the Internet.
splitz.description2: Creating Splitz wasn't just about tidying up my tabs, however; it was also about my commitment to continual learning and professional growth. As my first personal project, this experience fundamentally changed how I viewed software engineering, making me realize the endless potential that lies in creating things that seamlessly work together on the web.

splitz.feature2Body: Easily move tabs into the right category with a simple drag and drop.
splitz.feature3Body: Quickly switch between categories and manage tabs using shortcuts.
splitz.feature4Body: Choose between light and dark themes for a comfortable experience.
splitz.why1: I built Splitz to solve a problem I faced every day: too many open tabs and no good way to organize them.
splitz.why2: This project taught me how powerful small tools can be when they solve real problems. It was my first personal project, and publishing it on the Chrome Web Store was a major milestone in my journey as a developer.

utat.title: Low Power Sensor for Rocket Ground Station
utat.hero: A low-power sensor designed for the Defiance Rocket Project ground station to protect critical systems by automatically shutting down when the 22V battery voltage drops to 18V, minimizing power draw and preserving essential components.
utat.overview1: Developed for the Defiance Rocket Project, this low-power sensor monitors the ground station’s 22V battery and automatically disconnects the circuit when the voltage drops to 18V. This protects sensitive components from undervoltage conditions and reduces unnecessary power consumption once the system is shut down.
utat.overview2: The design emphasizes simplicity, reliability, and minimal current draw in the off state, which are critical for mission readiness and long-duration ground operations.
utat.requirement1Body: Turn off the circuit when the 22V battery voltage reaches 18V to protect components.
utat.requirement2Body: Ensure the circuit draws only a minimal amount of current after shutdown.
utat.approach: The circuit uses a precision voltage reference and comparator to monitor the battery voltage. When the battery drops to the 18V threshold, the comparator output drives the MOSFET gate to cut power to the load. A high-value resistor network keeps current draw extremely low once the circuit is off, helping preserve battery life and protect the rocket ground station’s electronics.
utat.stackIntro: Tools and languages used for the low-power sensor project.

fps.title: FPS Game
fps.subtitle: A Retro Ray-Traced Experiment in Low-Level Game Development
fps.hero: A first-person shooter built from the ground up in C for the Altera DE1-SoC board. The game renders a 3D maze-like environment from a 2D map using a lightweight ray-tracing approach, with player movement, collision detection, enemy sprites, fireballs, and VGA output all handled directly through low-level hardware interaction.
fps.sourceBody: This project is hosted in a private repository to support academic integrity.
fps.overview1: Developed for the University of Toronto's second-year Computer Engineering course, Computer Organization (ECE243), this project was my first complete game development experience and an introduction to graphics programming. The game uses a ray-based rendering system to project a simple 2D map into a first-person 3D view, drawing walls, floors, enemies, and projectiles in real time.
fps.overview2: The project was designed specifically for the Altera DE1-SoC board, using memory-mapped I/O to read hardware switches and push buttons, drive LED feedback, and render directly to the VGA pixel buffer. Beyond the visual renderer, the game includes player navigation, wall collision handling, sprite-based enemies, projectile firing, depth-based occlusion, and double-buffered rendering for smoother gameplay.
fps.contribution1: Implemented a ray tracing engine in C for a 3D FPS game
fps.contribution2: Developed hardware-level input handling through DE1-SoC switches and push buttons for movement, rotation, strafing, shooting, and game-state control
fps.contribution3: Implemented distance-based wall and floor shading to create depth, perspective, and a clearer sense of movement through the environment
fps.contribution4: Created sprite-based game objects for enemies and fireballs, including sampling logic, screen projection, object movement, and visibility checks
fps.contribution5: Implemented collision behavior for both the player and moving objects, including wall blocking, projectile removal, and enemy movement reversal
fps.contribution6: Tuned rendering resolution, movement speed, field of view, and distance stepping to balance performance and playability on limited embedded hardware
fps.renderingBody: The game renders its 3D view by casting rays across the player’s field of view and stepping each ray forward until it reaches a wall or exceeds the visible depth range. The measured distance is then used to determine the height and shade of each wall column, creating a first-person perspective from a 16x16 map.
fps.controlsBody: Player input is mapped directly to the board's physical switches and push buttons. The switches control movement, rotation, and strafing, while push buttons handle shooting and game-state actions.
fps.objectsBody: The game includes two main object types: enemy sprites and fireball projectiles. Both types of objects are updated every frame, checked against the map for wall collisions, projected into screen space, and drawn only when they fall inside the player’s field of view.
fps.vgaBody: The game outputs directly to a VGA display and is optimized to run reliably within the limited resources of the DE1-SoC platform. The final result is intentionally minimal, but technically complete: a playable FPS-style renderer built close to the hardware.
fps.arcadeBody: Inspired by early arcade shooters, this project captures the spirit of building a game from limited resources. The visuals are simple and the controls hardware-driven, but the project brings together the essential parts of an FPS: movement, perspective, enemies, collision, and real-time display.
fps.stackIntro: Tools and hardware used to build, test, and tune the FPS for real-time execution on the DE1-SoC board. The source code is private to support academic integrity.

mappa.hero: A lightweight geographic information system (GIS) application that helps users search for locations, compute optimal routes, and visualize spatial data with an interactive and fully customizable map experience.
mappa.overview: Mappa is a desktop GIS application built in C++ with the OpenStreetMap API and EZGL graphics library, allowing users to load and interact with global city maps in real time. The project was designed around the challenge of turning complex geographic data into an experience that feels clear, responsive, and easy to control. Through efficient map rendering, intuitive search, route-finding, and customizable visual layers, Mappa makes spatial information more accessible without sacrificing performance or usability.
mappa.highlight1: Fast and intelligent search with partial and misspelled-name support
mappa.highlight2: Locate intersections and compute shortest paths
mappa.highlight3: Delete past search data to keep the map clean and responsive
mappa.highlight4: 100% customizable map with colour schemes and filters
mappa.highlight5: Clear visual hierarchy with zoom-aware details and directions
mappa.engineering: This project was developed as part of a collaborative second-year engineering course, ECE297, at the University of Toronto. The course gave students the opportunity to design, build, and iterate on a complex software system from the ground up, applying core concepts in data structures, algorithms, graphics, and software design.

mappa.feature1Point2: Fast map loading and smooth navigation across large urban areas
mappa.feature1Point3: Responsive panning, zooming, and selection for an intuitive experience
mappa.feature2Point1: Implemented Dijkstra's and A* to compute optimal routes
mappa.feature2Point2: Supports complex travel queries with high accuracy and efficiency
mappa.feature2Point3: Visualizes shortest paths with distance and estimated travel time
mappa.feature3Point1: Customize colour schemes and map style

capstone.hero: A healthcare record system that puts patients at the center, protects sensitive data, and builds trust through blockchain technology.
capstone.builtForBody: Designed to support secure health data exchange across healthcare organizations.
capstone.flow2Body: Encrypted files are stored on IPFS.
capstone.flow3Body: Transactions are recorded on Hyperledger Fabric.
capstone.overview: HealthChainON is a blockchain-powered proof of concept for a secure, interoperable, and patient-centric electronic health record (EHR) system in Ontario. It was designed to explore how blockchain technology could address limitations in traditional EHR systems by improving transparency, strengthening patient control, and creating a more accountable way for health information to be stored, accessed, and shared.
capstone.problem: Ontario's health record systems remain fragmented across different healthcare providers, making it difficult for patients to access, control, and share their complete medical history. Records are often stored by individual institutions, which can lead to repeated data collection, delayed access, duplicated tests, and incomplete information during care. Existing EHR platforms improve parts of this process, but they do not fully solve three core issues:
capstone.pillar1Body: Patients often lack direct control over where their records are stored, who can access them, and how easily they can share them across providers.
capstone.pillar2Body: Health records contain sensitive personal information that must be protected from unauthorized access, tampering, and improper disclosure.
capstone.pillar3Body: Healthcare providers often rely on separate systems, making it difficult to exchange records cleanly across hospitals, labs, clinics, and patients.
capstone.blockchainIntro: Blockchain is an electronic ledger where transactions are grouped into blocks and linked through cryptographic hashes, creating a secure and tamper-evident record of activity. Because health records contain highly sensitive personal information, they require a system that can verify access, preserve a reliable history of actions, and reduce dependence on any single institution to control patient data. Blockchain supports this by providing a transparent, immutable, and decentralized foundation for managing trusted record activity.
capstone.reason1Body: All transactions are visible and verifiable across the network, ensuring that information flows openly and can be independently validated. This enhances accountability and prevents information blockage.
capstone.reason2Body: Once a record is written to the blockchain, it cannot be altered or deleted. This preserves the integrity of past records, ensuring a trustworthy history and preventing information corruption.
capstone.reason3Body: Data is distributed across multiple nodes rather than stored in a single central authority. This removes single points of failure, reduces dependency on one entity, and improves resilience and information security.
capstone.architectureIntro: HealthChainON is organized around a Web API that connects the user-facing application to the system’s storage, encryption, and blockchain components.
capstone.module1Body: Web interface for users to interact with the system securely.
capstone.module2Body: AES256 + HMAC encryption for secure file and data protection.
capstone.module3Body: Decentralized file storage for encrypted health records.
capstone.module4Body: Permissioned blockchain layer for immutable and verifiable records.
capstone.module5Body: Exposes blockchain functions through a RESTful API.
capstone.contributionsIntro: Four key areas where I led development and delivered impact.
capstone.contribution1Body: Researched Hyperledger Fabric's architecture, transaction flow, user authentication model, and chaincode execution process to define how a permissioned blockchain layer could support the application.
capstone.contribution2Body: Configured and adapted a Hyperledger Fabric sample network for the project by modifying organizations, removing unnecessary resources, and resolving compatibility issues so the blockchain layer could support healthcare record workflows.
capstone.contribution3Body: Implemented the blockchain business logic for registration, authentication, record transactions, and data retrieval, creating 16 deterministic chaincode functions for network validation.
capstone.contribution4Body: Built a 14-endpoint API that connected the web application to the Hyperledger Fabric chaincode, exposed blockchain actions to the front end, and enforced JWT-based role access control.
capstone.posterIntro: The scientific poster created for the capstone presentation and evaluation.
capstone.stackIntro: Technologies and tools used across the system.

aps360.title: Song Popularity Predictor
aps360.description: With the exponential growth of music streaming services, breaking into the music industry has become increasingly challenging for new artists. As streaming platforms like Spotify rely heavily on algorithms that recommend songs based on their perceived popularity, it has become crucial for artists to create music that aligns with these algorithmic preferences. The objective of this project was to develop a predictive model that could forecast the popularity of a song based on its audio features. By leveraging deep learning techniques, specifically an Artificial Neural Network (ANN), this project aimed to provide artists with valuable insights into which songs are likely to gain the most exposure on streaming platforms, thereby improving their chances of success in a competitive industry.
aps360.data1: The foundation of any predictive model lies in the quality and relevance of the data used for training. For this project, we utilized a combination of a pre-existing dataset from Kaggle and song features extracted directly from the Spotify API. The initial dataset comprised 174,000 songs, but our group applied several processing steps to refine this data to better suit our model's requirements.
aps360.data2: The first step involved filtering out any songs released before the year 2000, as our focus was on current music trends. This reduced the dataset to 42,000 songs. We then eliminated any duplicate songs to prevent the model from being biased towards certain feature values. In cases where duplicates existed, the most popular version of the song was retained. This further refined the dataset to approximately 38,000 songs. To ensure the model could train effectively, we calculated the mean, median, and mode of the dataset’s popularity scores, aiming for a balanced distribution around a mean popularity rating of 50. Finally, we applied min-max normalization to all data values, standardizing them between 0 and 1. This normalization was crucial for speeding up the model's learning process and handling the variability between different feature values. Additionally, we implemented a weighted cross-entropy function to address class imbalance, ensuring the model did not favor any particular class.
aps360.model1: The heart of this project was the development and training of a deep learning model using an Artificial Neural Network (ANN). The choice of an ANN was driven by its ability to learn complex, non-linear relationships between input features and the target output—in this case, the song's popularity.
aps360.model2: The architecture of our ANN consisted of four fully connected layers. The first three layers were composed of 1,000, 2,000, and 4,000 hidden units, respectively, and utilized the ReLU activation function. This setup allowed the model to capture intricate patterns in the data by assigning weights to different song features. The output layer consisted of five neurons, each corresponding to a specific popularity class ranging from 0 to 4. These classes were designed to simplify the prediction process and reduce variance, making it easier for the model to achieve accurate results. Our model was trained over multiple epochs, and we carefully tuned hyperparameters to achieve the best possible performance.
aps360.results1: The ANN model we developed demonstrated significant improvements over the baseline model—a decision tree classifier. While the decision tree achieved a baseline accuracy of 45%, our ANN model outperformed it with a testing accuracy of 55%. To further evaluate the model's performance, we also examined its accuracy across different popularity classes. The model excelled in predicting songs in the mid-range popularity classes (2 and 3), achieving accuracies of 53.4% and 58.8%, respectively. However, it struggled with songs at the extremes of the popularity spectrum, particularly in classes 1 and 4, where accuracy dropped significantly. Despite these challenges, the model provided valuable insights into the relationship between a song's audio features and its potential success on streaming platforms.
aps360.results2: Overall, this project showcased the potential of applying deep learning to predict song popularity. As my first AI-related project, it was both challenging and rewarding, resulting in a model that outperformed traditional methods and provided valuable insights. This experience deepened my interest in AI and its practical applications in the music industry and beyond.
